meanings.meaning: "Within your gates" means in the cities, towns, and villages of your land, not just inside your own house. So the foreigner within your gates is a foreign worker who has settled among the Israelites.

idioms.idiom: cut off from among his people

meanings.meaning: A man who killed an ox, lamb, or goat without bringing it to God's tent was treated like a murderer. He was removed from his people, perhaps by death from the leaders or from God.
It means worshiping the false god Molech. God had joined Israel to Himself like a husband to a wife, so serving another god was like being unfaithful in marriage.
God punishes those who hate Him openly and quickly, without putting it off. Bible teachers say this may mean in their own lifetime, or right before Him, since they sin boldly.
To be the apple of His eye is to be guarded very carefully by God. Here God led Israel safely through the dangerous wilderness and protected His special people.

idioms.idiom: march in and out with me

meanings.meaning: It means all of David's behavior as a soldier with Achish. Achish was saying David had acted well in the army and he could find nothing wrong with him.
Bible teachers disagree. Some say the dew means the king's young men, who come to him gladly like fresh morning dew, while others say it means the king's own youthful strength.

idioms.idiom: For three transgressions of Israel, even four

meanings.meaning: This isn't an exact count. God is saying Israel sinned again and again, so He will not hold back His punishment, since judges let bribes, even tiny ones, decide against honest and poor people.
To "fall away" on account of Jesus means to be put off by Him and start to doubt or turn away from Him. Jesus says the person who does not doubt Him is blessed.

idioms.idiom: He is at my right hand

meanings.meaning: God is right beside Him, close and ready to help and protect Him, like a helper standing at His side to defend Him. So He will not be shaken.

idioms.idiom: It is hard for you to kick against the goads

meanings.meaning: Jesus was scolding Saul for stubbornly resisting what he already felt was true in his heart. Saul was fighting against his own convictions on purpose.
Giving the right hand was a sign of trust, friendship, and partnership. The church leaders welcomed Paul and Barnabas as fellow workers who preached the same gospel as they did.

idioms.idiom: seated at the right hand of God

meanings.meaning: Christ has the highest place of honor beside God in heaven. He has gone ahead to prepare heavenly happiness for His people.

left_out.idiom: He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The commentary notes given are cut off before they reach the part about visiting the fathers' iniquity on the children. They explain only that God forgives sin yet does not leave the guilty unpunished. Nothing in them explains how the children are affected, so a meaning would require adding outside information.

left_out.idiom: grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The notes do not explain the grass-on-the-rooftops image. Keil and Delitzsch's note is cut off before it reaches that part of verse 26. Clarke only says God had made the people weak, so the Assyrian king beat them. The idiom list's meaning about thin roof soil and drying in the sun is not supported by the notes.

the notes don't explain it: The notes do not explain what 'Moab is My washbasin' means. Calvin only gives the verse (as 'the pot of my washing') and points back to Psalm 60. Matthew Henry says only that David looks on Moab, Edom and Philistia as already his, because God promised him victory over his enemies. He says nothing about a washbasin. Clarke and Gill add nothing about this phrase. The idea of a menial servant people in the idiom list is not supported by the notes.

left_out.idiom: upon Edom I toss My sandal
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: None of the commentary notes explain what tossing a sandal over Edom means. Matthew Henry only says David looks on Moab, Edom and Philistia as already his, because God promised him victory over his enemies. Calvin points to Psalms 57 and 60 without explaining it. Keil and Delitzsch only discuss Hebrew wording, and Adam Clarke's note is about a different line. The idea of a slave, taking land, or trampling is not in the notes.

left_out.idiom: His winnowing fork is in His hand
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The notes given do not explain the winnowing fork image. Calvin's note is cut off before it reaches verse 17's meaning, and it only says Christ is greater than John. Gill and Clarke only point to other passages (Matthew 3:12 and others) that are not included. Matthew Henry's note is also cut off and does not explain the fork. Without that, any meaning would come from outside knowledge.

left_out.idiom: let this cup pass from Me
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The notes given do not explain what the cup means. Calvin's text only repeats the verses, and Gill's note covers falling on one's face and calling God Father. Neither says what the cup stands for. The idiom list meaning is about Jeremiah 49:12 and cannot be confirmed from these notes.
